theme: Friendship introduces Xenophon to an army; leadership entails care for other people

reading.title: Φίλος ἐν τῇ στρατιᾷ
reading.audioPlaceholder: Reading audio has not yet been recorded.
introduction: Lesson 12 ended with Socrates’s response to Xenophon’s decision. Here the expedition begins: Xenophon catches up with Proxenus and Cyrus at Sardis as the army prepares to march.

Source: Anabasis 1.2.1–5 supplies the gathering contingents; 3.1.4 and 3.1.8–10 supply Xenophon’s initial status, arrival, introduction, and limited knowledge of the objective. The greeting, camp observations, and private question below are educational reconstruction. The final companion paragraph adapts Memorabilia 3.2.1–4 as a separate Socratic teaching, without asserting that Xenophon remembered this exchange at Sardis.

This is adapted Attic Greek in the historical present, not an extract of Xenophon’s wording. Blue glosses support names and constructions beyond the lesson. No future, aorist, or participle is a production target here.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ξενοφῶν εἰς Σάρδεις ἀφικνεῖται. ἐκεῖ ὁ Κῦρος καὶ ὁ Πρόξενος τὴν στρατιὰν παρασκευάζονται. ὁ Ξενοφῶν πρὸς τὸν φίλον ἔρχεται· νῦν ἡ μακρὰ ὁδὸς ἄρχεται.

gloss.english: at Sardis; accusative plural place name

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Πρόξενος τὸν Ξενοφῶντα δέχεται καὶ λέγει· «ὦ φίλε, χαίρειν. ὅδε ὁ στρατηγὸς Κῦρός ἐστιν.» ὁ Κῦρος τὸν Ξενοφῶντα δέχεται καὶ πρὸς τὴν στρατιὰν καλεῖ.
Ὁ Ξενοφῶν οὔτε στρατηγός ἐστιν οὔτε λοχαγὸς οὔτε στρατιώτης. διὰ τὴν φιλίαν τοῦ Προξένου πάρεστιν. φίλος στρατηγοῦ ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ τῶν στρατιωτῶν οὐκ ἄρχει.

gloss.english: does not command the soldiers; ἄρχω takes genitive

paragraphs.greek: Πολλοὶ Ἕλληνες ἐν Σάρδεσιν εἰσίν. ὁ μὲν Ξενίας ὁπλίτας ἄγει, ὁ δὲ Πρόξενος ὁπλίτας καὶ ψιλοὺς ἔχει. ἄλλοι στρατηγοὶ τὰ ἑαυτῶν στρατεύματα ἄγουσιν· οὐ πάντες ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς χώρας ἔρχονται.

gloss.english: not all; πᾶς is formally taught in Lesson 16

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ξενοφῶν τοὺς φύλακας καὶ τὰ ὅπλα βλέπει. οἱ φύλακες τὰ σώματα γυμνάζουσι καὶ τὰ τοῦ στρατοπέδου πράγματα φυλάττουσιν. οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι οὐ μόνον ἑαυτοὺς σῴζουσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς φίλους.
Ὁ Κῦρος περὶ τῶν Πισιδῶν λέγει. ὁ Ξενοφῶν τὸν λόγον ἀκούει, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἀληθῆ σκοπὸν τῆς πορείας οὐ γιγνώσκει. ἡ φιλία τοῦ Προξένου οὐ πάντα δηλοῖ.

gloss.english: about the Pisidians; people of inland Anatolia
the true objective; untaught adjective form
not everything; neuter plural of πᾶς

paragraphs.greek: Ἐν τῷ στρατοπέδῳ ὁ Ξενοφῶν σκέπτεται· «ἐγὼ ἐμαυτὸν παρασκευάζω. ὁ δὲ στρατηγὸς οὐ μόνον ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιμελεῖται. τοὺς ἄλλους φυλάττει. ἆρα ὁ ἀγαθὸς στρατηγὸς καὶ ἀγαθὸς φύλαξ ἐστίν;»

gloss.english: looks after himself; ἐπιμελέομαι takes genitive

paragraphs.greek: Ἕτερος λόγος τοῦ Σωκράτους περὶ ἀρχῆς ἐστιν. ὁ Σωκράτης τὸν στρατηγὸν ποιμένα τῶν στρατιωτῶν καλεῖ. ὁ ποιμὴν τὰ πρόβατα σῴζει· ὁ δὲ στρατηγὸς τοὺς στρατιώτας φυλάττει καὶ τροφὴν παρασκευάζει. οἱ ἀγαθοὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιμελοῦνται.

gloss.english: care for others; contracted deponent plus genitive

reading.translation:
Xenophon arrives at Sardis. There Cyrus and Proxenus are preparing the army. Xenophon comes to his friend; now the long journey begins.

Proxenus welcomes Xenophon and says: “Greetings, my friend. This commander is Cyrus.” Cyrus welcomes Xenophon and invites him to join the army.

Xenophon is neither a general nor a captain nor an ordinary soldier. He is present because of his friendship with Proxenus. He is a friend of a general, but he does not command the soldiers.

Many Greeks are at Sardis. Xenias leads hoplites, while Proxenus has hoplites and light-armed men. Other generals lead their own contingents; they do not all come from the same country.

Xenophon sees the guards and the weapons. The guards train their bodies and protect the camp’s possessions. The brave protect not only themselves but also their friends.

Cyrus speaks about the Pisidians. Xenophon hears the account, but does not know the journey’s true objective. Friendship with Proxenus does not reveal everything.

In the camp Xenophon reflects: “I prepare myself. But the general does not look after only himself. He protects the others. Is a good general also a good guardian?”

A separate account of Socrates concerns leadership. Socrates calls the general a shepherd of the soldiers. A shepherd keeps the sheep safe; a general protects the soldiers and provides food. Good people care for others.

blocks.title: Words in the Reading
body: φύλαξ is a guard or guardian, and φυλάττω means protect or guard. Read the shared φυλακ-/φυλαττ- family as a meaning connection, not as a rule for mechanically making one word from the other. The genitive φύλακος shows the noun’s velar stem.

στρατηγός names a general; λοχαγός names a company commander; στρατιώτης names a soldier. Xenophon explicitly places himself outside all three roles at the beginning. Being a commander’s friend does not supply command authority.
ἑαυτοῦ points back to the subject. Contrast care for oneself with τῶν ἄλλων, care for other people. Our narrative question joins the word families of protection and responsibility.

grammar.intro: Substantive adjectives; declension systems; velar and dental stems; reflexive pronouns. Work through each section, use its checks and topic practice, then complete the grammar exercises. Reading-only forms remain supported by glosses.
objectives: Interpret adjectives used as nouns for people or things.
Use dictionary nominative, genitive, and article to establish stem, declension, and gender.
Decline φύλαξ and σῶμα and explain velar/dental changes.
Identify the subject referred to by reflexive pronouns and choose agreement and case.

sections.title: 1. Adjectives That Name People
body: An adjective can stand with the article without an expressed noun. οἱ ἀγαθοί means “the good people”; οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι means “the brave.” The article and adjective still carry gender, number, and case.

Masculine plural often refers to people; a neuter form can name things or qualities, as τὸ ἀγαθόν, “the good thing” or “what is good.” Context supplies the omitted noun. Do not insert “soldiers” unless the context warrants it.

In οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι τοὺς φίλους σῴζουσιν, the nominative article shows that the brave are the subject; τοὺς φίλους is the object. The grammar identifies the group, while the sentence defines its responsibility.

examples.english: He brings food to the good people.

checks.prompt: Who acts in οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι σῴζουσιν?
checks.answer: The brave people; the article and adjective are nominative plural.

sections.title: 2. Reading a Dictionary Entry
body: A noun entry gives the nominative, genitive, and article: φύλαξ, φύλακος, ὁ. The article supplies gender. The genitive reveals the stem and declension pattern; remove -ος from φύλακος to find φυλακ-.

First-declension nouns commonly have genitives in -ας or -ης; second-declension nouns normally have -ου. Third-declension consonant stems normally have -ος. Gender and declension are different information: a third-declension noun may be masculine, feminine, or neuter.

Keep familiar first/second endings available while learning new stems. Nominative names the subject, genitive commonly possession, dative a recipient or related person, and accusative the direct object. A stem is a building base, not a complete word to translate on its own.

sections.title: 3. Velar and Dental Stems
body: Velars κ, γ, χ combine with nominative -ς or dative plural -σι to produce ξ: φυλακ- + ς → φύλαξ; φυλακ- + σι → φύλαξι. The oblique cases show κ clearly: φύλακος, φύλακα, φύλακες.

Dental stems end in τ, δ, or θ. A dental disappears before σ. Neuter σῶμα has stem σωματ-, visible in σώματος and σώματα. Its nominative/accusative singular has no -ς and drops final τ; dative plural σωματ- + σι becomes σώμασι.

All neuters have identical nominative and accusative forms. The plural ends in -α. Third-declension masculine/feminine accusative singular often ends in -α, while the plural ends in -ας. Movable ν may follow dative plural -σι.

checks.prompt: Why is φύλαξι written with ξ?
checks.answer: Stem κ combines with σ of -σι to produce ξ.

sections.title: 4. Referring Back to the Subject
body: A reflexive refers back to the subject of its clause: ὁ στρατηγὸς ἑαυτὸν σῴζει, “the general saves himself.” Compare αὐτὸν σῴζει, “he saves him,” where him ordinarily points to another person. Reflexives have no nominative because they are not the clause’s subject.

Singular first person uses ἐμαυτοῦ, second person σεαυτοῦ, and third person ἑαυτοῦ. Gender follows the person referred to, while case comes from the pronoun’s role. A woman as subject requires ἑαυτήν in the accusative, for example.

The plural third-person forms are ἑαυτῶν, ἑαυτοῖς/ἑαυταῖς, ἑαυτούς/ἑαυτάς. They can serve all three persons in a plural reflexive context. Care verbs such as ἐπιμελέομαι take the genitive: ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιμελεῖται, “he cares for himself.”

checks.prompt: Who is saved in ὁ στρατηγὸς ἑαυτὸν σῴζει?
checks.answer: The general himself, the same person as the subject.

summary.title: Grammar Summary
items: An article plus an adjective can name a group: οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι, the brave.
A genitive reveals the stem; the dictionary article gives gender.
φυλακ- + σ → ξ; σωματ- loses τ before σ. Neuter nominative and accusative match.
A reflexive points back to the subject and has the case its construction requires.

sections.title: An army gathered by personal networks
body: Anabasis 1.2.1–5 presents Cyrus collecting forces from several sources. The Greeks at Sardis belong to distinct contingents with their own commanders; Proxenus brings heavy and light infantry. The army’s organization is more complex than a single city sending its citizen force. Cyrus’s announced target is the Pisidians, while Tissaphernes suspects preparations on a larger scale.

Personal relationships make a practical difference. Anabasis 3.1.4 and 8–10 connects Xenophon’s arrival to Proxenus’s invitation and Cyrus’s welcome. Friendship provides access but does not automatically make the visitor a commander. Xenophon’s account of his early status matters when we later follow his assumption of responsibility.

sections.title: What a title does and does not establish
body: The reading distinguishes στρατηγός, general, from λοχαγός, commander of a company, and στρατιώτης, soldier. These are roles in an army’s hierarchy, not degrees of personal worth. Xenophon says he began as none of the three. The reconstructed camp scene lets readers notice guards, equipment, food, and preparation without inventing a formal military appointment for him.

The soldiers do not all possess the same information as Cyrus. Xenophon later says he himself was mistaken about the expedition’s objective. Reading a retrospective account requires attention to who knew what at a given moment. The Greek commanders’ recruitment and the author’s later explanation cannot be compressed into complete knowledge for everyone at Sardis.

sections.title: The shepherd comparison
body: In Memorabilia 3.2 Socrates discusses leadership with a man elected general and examines Homer’s image of a shepherd of the people. Care includes safety and supplies as well as military success. The leader’s excellence is judged partly by the condition of the people entrusted to him. The analogy does not erase the difference between human beings and sheep; it asks what responsibility a position entails.

This companion scene comes from another work and another setting. We use it to evaluate the expedition, not to claim that Xenophon witnessed or recalled the conversation at Sardis. A reflection question follows: if friendship brings someone close to power, what must he learn before he can care responsibly for people affected by that power?

questions.prompt: How is the Greek army at Sardis organized?
questions.answer: It contains contingents recruited under different commanders.

questions.prompt: What stated target does Cyrus offer?
questions.answer: The Pisidians; the wider objective is not yet openly announced to the Greeks.

questions.prompt: What is Xenophon’s initial military office?
questions.answer: He says he is neither general, captain, nor ordinary soldier.

questions.prompt: Does friendship with Proxenus establish command authority?
questions.answer: No. It explains access and participation, not a formal appointment.

questions.prompt: What does the shepherd comparison emphasize?
questions.answer: A leader should care for the safety, supplies, and welfare of those entrusted to him.

questions.prompt: Why is the Socratic passage separate?
questions.answer: It is a comparison from Memorabilia, not an attested camp conversation or memory.

review.title: Before the Final Quiz
items: An article plus an adjective can name a group: οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι, the brave.
A genitive reveals the stem; the dictionary article gives gender.
φυλακ- + σ → ξ; σωματ- loses τ before σ. Neuter nominative and accusative match.
A reflexive points back to the subject and has the case its construction requires.
